first_impression.reaction: This sounds like our house. James's mum keeps asking who our ninong and ninang will be and we honestly didn't know what that meant. The intro asks exactly those questions, doesn't oversell, and says up front that families have their own versions. That earns a proper read, not a skim.

journey.quote: Filipino wedding traditions are rarely written down in one place, and most families hold their own version.
journey.reaction: Honest. It isn't pretending there's one correct way, which is what I'd say to James's mum to keep the peace.

journey.section: Filipino wedding traditions at a glance
journey.quote: The table below is a starting point, not a script.
journey.reaction: The table is the bit I'd screenshot and send to James and both sets of parents. When, who, done. Really useful.

journey.quote: For a destination wedding, a practical note: hold the pamamanhikan, or a version of it over dinner, before you lock the date.
journey.reaction: This is the kind of advice I actually want: a real step that keeps the older generation on side. It feels like someone who has done this before.

journey.quote: If a grandparent raises one, it is usually easier to listen and adjust a small detail than to argue the point.
journey.reaction: Ha. Yes. Sensible, warm, not preachy.

journey.quote: Brief them on timing at the rehearsal, because the three rites follow on from each other quickly.
journey.reaction: Insider detail. But if our sponsors are flying in from Manila and Sydney for a wedding in Europe, who briefs them and who makes sure the veil and cord actually turn up? The post stops right before the part I'd pay someone for.

journey.quote: Philippine law requires no prescribed form or religious rite for a marriage, so a couple can keep any of these as cultural moments wherever they marry.
journey.reaction: Good, that tells me we can do the veil and cord in a celebrant ceremony in Italy or wherever we land. Big relief for us.

journey.quote: If guests from outside the culture are coming, a line on the wedding website explaining the dance spares everyone a moment of confusion.
journey.reaction: Half our friends would have no idea. This is exactly the 'don't look awkward in front of our friends' worry handled nicely.

journey.quote: For a sense of how this looks away from the Philippines, see a Filipino couple's autumn wedding in Tuscany.
journey.reaction: A real wedding with a real place. That's the link I'd click next, and it's the kind of thing that moves us towards enquiring.

journey.quote: Grooms in a suit for the ceremony sometimes change into a barong for dinner.
journey.reaction: Nice idea, but where do we get a proper barong made if we're in Sydney and marrying overseas? No hint at all.

journey.section: Documents and steps from official sources
journey.quote: Not published: a single official checklist of documents and timelines for Australians marrying in the Philippines. Your Wedded Advisor confirms current requirements with you in writing.
journey.reaction: I'm a lawyer. Being told plainly that there is no single checklist, and that someone will confirm it in writing, is worth more to me than a made-up list. That's one of the most reassuring lines on the page.

journey.quote: Shortlist only places outside the higher-level areas, and recheck Smartraveller advice for the Philippines before you pay any deposits, since the page is updated regularly.
journey.reaction: Dated, sourced, practical. Mum will ask about safety the second we mention the Philippines, and I can just forward this.

journey.quote: One person works with you in your time zone, from first idea to the last dance.
journey.reaction: Better than 'end-to-end', but it's still a slogan. What does that one person actually do with our 40 overseas guests and our grandparents getting from the airport? Tell me one concrete thing.

journey.section: Bringing Filipino traditions into your celebration
journey.quote: The conversations with parents and grandparents along the way are often the part that is remembered longest.
journey.reaction: Lovely and true, without being schmaltzy. No fairytale talk anywhere, which I appreciated.

unanswered_questions: If we marry outside the Philippines (say Italy), can Wedded Wonderland find a celebrant or priest who knows the veil, cord and arras rites, or do we have to brief them ourselves?
Who sources the veil, cord, arras and a properly made barong and Filipiniana if we are based in Sydney?
How do you look after older relatives and sponsors flying in from the Philippines, including visas and airport transfers?
What does the Wedded Advisor actually handle day to day, and who is accountable on the wedding day itself?
Is the Tuscany couple's wedding one you planned, and can we see how the Filipino customs were run there?
would_share_with: James's mum, for the sponsors and pamamanhikan sections
My parents, for the Smartraveller section

cta_reaction.quote: When you are ready to talk dates, families and paperwork, your Wedded Advisor is one conversation away.
cta_reaction.why: It's soft and not pushy, which I like. But I'm 14 months out with no destination, and I'd only enquire after reading the Tuscany real wedding and one or two more posts. Nothing here would stop me enquiring later; it just doesn't yet show me what you'd do that I can't do myself with a spreadsheet.

top_3_changes: Add one short, concrete paragraph on running these rites at a destination outside the Philippines: who briefs sponsors, who brings the veil, cord and arras, and how the celebrant is prepared.

Replace or back up 'One person works with you in your time zone, from first idea to the last dance' with one specific thing the Wedded Advisor does, for example coordinating travelling sponsors and elderly relatives.
Point more clearly to the Tuscany real wedding (and say whether Wedded Wonderland planned it) near the close, since that is the step that moves us towards enquiring.
